statements: In adults with multiple coronary risk factors but no evident coronary heart disease (CHD), reduces myocardial infarction, stroke, revascularization, and angina risk. In adults with type 2 diabetes and multiple CHD risk factors but no evident CHD, reduces myocardial infarction and stroke risk. In established CHD, reduces nonfatal myocardial infarction, fatal and nonfatal stroke, revascularization, heart-failure hospitalization, and angina risk.

As an adjunct to diet, lowers LDL-C in adults with primary hyperlipidemia and in patients aged 10 years or older with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH). Also treats adult hypertriglyceridemia and primary dysbetalipoproteinemia. For homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HoFH) from age 10, use with other LDL-lowering treatment, or alone if those treatments are unavailable.

This profile summarizes Lipitor tablets. Other brands, generic labels, combination medicines, and alternative dosage forms may have different labeled uses or instructions. It does not provide an exhaustive off-label treatment guide.
Adults: Start 10–20 mg once daily; range 10–80 mg once daily. A 40 mg start may be used when LDL-C reduction greater than 45% is needed.
HeFH · age ≥10 years: Start 10 mg once daily; range 10–20 mg once daily.
HoFH · age ≥10 years: Start 10–20 mg once daily; range 10–80 mg once daily.
Take tablets once daily at any time, with or without food. Skip a missed dose and resume the next scheduled dose.
Assess LDL-C as clinically appropriate, as early as 4 weeks after starting, and adjust to response. Interaction-related limits may be lower than the usual maximum.

Renal impairment does not require a dose adjustment, but increases muscle-injury risk. Chronic alcohol-associated liver disease markedly increases exposure. Acute liver failure and decompensated cirrhosis are contraindications; assess other hepatic disease individually rather than applying a universal dose reduction.

Atorvaliq is a 20 mg/5 mL (4 mg/mL) suspension taken on an empty stomach, 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal. Shake well before each use. Measure with a calibrated oral device in mL. Its missed-dose directions allow taking a dose as soon as possible unless more than 12 hours late; then skip it. Follow its own storage instructions. Lipitor tablet directions do not apply.
Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis can cause acute kidney injury and rarely death. Risk increases with age ≥65, uncontrolled hypothyroidism, renal impairment, interacting medicines, and higher doses.

Discontinue when myopathy is diagnosed or suspected or CK is markedly elevated. Temporarily interrupt during serious acute illness with high risk of renal failure from rhabdomyolysis. Persistent weakness and elevated CK after stopping may indicate immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, requiring further evaluation.
Consider liver enzymes before treatment and when clinically indicated. Promptly discontinue for serious liver injury with symptoms, jaundice, or hyperbilirubinemia. Glucose and HbA1c can rise.

The 80 mg dose warrants individualized benefit–risk review after a recent hemorrhagic stroke. The label reports an increased hemorrhagic-stroke signal in a post-hoc analysis of SPARCL; do not generalize it to every patient or dose.

Acute liver failure, decompensated cirrhosis, or hypersensitivity to atorvastatin or product ingredients. Pregnancy is no longer listed as an absolute contraindication; see population-specific guidance.
The selected Lipitor tablet label has no boxed warning. Its warnings and precautions still require attention to muscle injury, hepatic injury, and relevant population and interaction risks.
Common trial reports included nasopharyngitis, joint pain, diarrhea, extremity pain, and urinary tract infection.
Serious reactions include muscle injury, hepatic injury, and hypersensitivity. Trial frequencies depend on study design and are not comparative risk estimates across statins.
Not recommended: Cyclosporine; gemfibrozil; tipranavir/ritonavir; glecaprevir/pibrentasvir.
Maximum 20 mg daily: Clarithromycin; itraconazole; saquinavir/ritonavir; darunavir/ritonavir; fosamprenavir with or without ritonavir; elbasvir/grazoprevir; letermovir.
Maximum 40 mg daily: Nelfinavir.
Individual benefit–risk assessment: Lopinavir/ritonavir; simeprevir; ledipasvir/sofosbuvir; other azole antifungals or macrolides. Monitor for muscle toxicity.

Fibrates other than gemfibrozil, lipid-modifying niacin (≥1 g/day), and colchicine add muscle risk; weigh benefit and monitor if combined. Avoid large grapefruit-juice quantities (>1.2 L/day). Give rifampin simultaneously with Lipitor because delayed dosing can reduce atorvastatin exposure. Monitor digoxin appropriately; atorvastatin can raise norethindrone and ethinyl estradiol concentrations.
These are the selected label’s interaction instructions, not a complete screen for every newly prescribed medicine. Check both drug labels before adding treatment.

Stop treatment when pregnancy is recognized in most patients; the label permits consideration of ongoing therapeutic needs. FDA removed the class-wide pregnancy contraindication in 2021 to allow individualized decisions, particularly for very high-risk patients. Notify the prescriber promptly about a known or suspected pregnancy. Observational data have not established an increase in major birth defects; this does not establish safety for every pregnancy.

Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment. Discuss temporary treatment interruption versus continued statin therapy with alternative infant feeding based on the patient’s cardiovascular needs.
Lipitor HeFH and HoFH uses are established from age 10; safety and effectiveness below 10 or for other pediatric hyperlipidemias are not established.
Choose doses cautiously in older adults and monitor for muscle symptoms. Organ impairment and polypharmacy increase risk; see dosing for the relevant renal and hepatic distinctions.

Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, reducing cholesterol synthesis and increasing hepatic LDL-receptor-mediated clearance. LDL-C response guides dosing; plasma concentration alone is not the treatment target.
Absorption: Peak concentration in approximately 1–2 hours; parent-drug bioavailability about 14%.
Metabolism: CYP3A4; active metabolites contribute substantially to enzyme inhibition.
Elimination: Mainly biliary; less than 2% of a dose recovered in urine.
Half-life: Parent drug about 14 hours; inhibitory activity 20–30 hours with active metabolites.
Reassess LDL-C as early as 4 weeks after starting and adjust to the individualized plan.
Consider liver enzymes before treatment and thereafter when clinically indicated. Evaluate jaundice, dark urine, appetite loss, fatigue, or right-upper-abdominal discomfort.
Investigate unexplained muscle symptoms; CK and renal assessment are appropriate when muscle injury is suspected. Persistent weakness after stopping warrants assessment for immune-mediated myopathy.
Review glucose risk and reinforce healthy diet, activity, and weight management.
Use the prescribed once-daily schedule and avoid doubling missed doses.
Maintain diet and activity measures alongside drug treatment. Review all new medicines and supplements with the prescriber or pharmacist.
Promptly report unexplained muscle symptoms, especially with fever or feeling unwell. Seek urgent care for a severe allergic reaction.
Discuss pregnancy or breastfeeding promptly with the treating clinician.
For overdose, contact U.S. Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222; emergency symptoms require emergency care.
Other strengths and manufacturers have different appearances and package identifiers. Verify the exact imprint and original packaging with a pharmacist.

Label distributor: Viatris Specialty LLC

Follow the exact formulation’s storage instructions and retain packaging to identify the medicine.

assertions: Synthroid is prescription replacement therapy for congenital or acquired primary, secondary or tertiary hypothyroidism in adults and children, including neonates. It also supports surgery and radioiodine treatment of thyrotropin-dependent, well-differentiated thyroid cancer.

It is not indicated for benign thyroid-nodule or nontoxic diffuse-goiter suppression in iodine-sufficient patients, or for the recovery phase of subacute thyroiditis. Do not prescribe for weight loss in a euthyroid patient.
The linked ready-to-use injection is labeled for adult myxedema coma. Oral-to-IV equivalence is not established; specialist emergency care and the exact IV label are required.
Doses above 200 mcg/day are seldom needed. A poor response above 300 mcg/day warrants assessment of adherence, absorption and interactions. A dose may take 4–6 weeks to reach its peak effect.
Adults without a need for a reduced start | Full replacement is approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day; individualize. Adjust by 12.5–25 mcg every 4–6 weeks.

Older adults, atrial-fibrillation risk or cardiac disease | Start below the full replacement dose; titrate every 6–8 weeks. The current Synthroid label does not specify a universal fixed low starting dose.
Thyroid-cancer TSH suppression | Individualize to the target TSH for cancer stage and clinical status.

Adjust to laboratory results and development; usual pediatric titration is every 2 weeks. Infants at cardiac-failure risk start lower and increase every 4–6 weeks. For hyperactivity risk, the label starts at one-quarter of full replacement and increases by one-quarter weekly.
0–3 months | 10–15 mcg/kg
3–6 months | 8–10 mcg/kg
6–12 months | 6–8 mcg/kg
1–5 years | 5–6 mcg/kg
6–12 years | 4–5 mcg/kg
Over 12 years; growth/puberty incomplete | 2–3 mcg/kg
Growth/puberty complete | 1.6 mcg/kg

Take once daily on an empty stomach 30–60 minutes before breakfast. Separate absorption-interfering medicines by at least 4 hours; see the interaction card for resin-specific timing. For a child unable to swallow, freshly crush a tablet into 5–10 mL water, give immediately and ensure the full dose is swallowed. Do not store the mixture or mix into soy-based formula.

Check TSH and free T4 promptly when pregnancy is confirmed. For pre-existing primary disease with TSH above the trimester range, the label uses 12.5–25 mcg/day increases and TSH testing every 4 weeks until stable. For newly diagnosed disease, its starting doses are 1.6 mcg/kg/day if TSH ≥10 mIU/L and 1.0 mcg/kg/day if TSH <10 mIU/L. Return to the pre-pregnancy dose after delivery and check TSH at 4–8 weeks postpartum; individualize further changes.

The reviewed oral label supplies no fixed renal or hepatic dose-reduction formula. Dose to the disease-specific thyroid tests and clinical response; comorbid illness and altered hormone binding can complicate interpretation.
This is the Fresenius ready-to-use solution label, not a reconstitution instruction for powder products. Do not infer an exact oral-to-IV conversion.
Loading dose | 300–500 mcg IV; choose lower doses for older adults or cardiac disease.
Maintenance | 50–100 mcg IV daily until oral treatment is tolerated.
Administration | Do not exceed 100 mcg/min; do not add to IV fluids.

Over- or under-replacement can harm cardiac function, bone, growth, cognition and reproductive or metabolic function. Excess dosing can precipitate angina or atrial fibrillation, especially in older adults or cardiac disease.
Treat concomitant adrenal insufficiency with glucocorticoids before thyroid replacement to prevent adrenal crisis.
Monitor glucose when starting, changing or stopping therapy in diabetes. Excess replacement can lower bone density, particularly after menopause.
Myxedema coma is an emergency requiring an IV thyroid product; oral absorption is unreliable.

Uncorrected adrenal insufficiency is the reviewed label’s contraindication. Hypersensitivity reactions to inactive ingredients have been reported; select and evaluate formulations carefully after suspected allergy.
Thyroid hormone must not be used for obesity or weight loss. Doses exceeding physiological needs can cause life-threatening toxicity, particularly with sympathomimetic appetite suppressants.

Overdose-like hyperthyroid effects include tremor, heat intolerance, insomnia, sweating, diarrhea, palpitations and arrhythmias. Serious cardiac events, seizures and pediatric intracranial hypertension or growth-plate complications are reported. Excipient allergy can cause rash, wheezing or angioedema. Symptoms after an overdose may be delayed for days; seek urgent assessment and contact U.S. Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

Calcium, iron and phosphate binders: separate by at least 4 hours. Bile-acid sequestrants and ion-exchange resins: take Synthroid at least 4 hours before them or monitor TSH as specified by the label.
Antacids, sucralfate and acid suppression can reduce absorption; review timing and monitor thyroid response. Orlistat also requires thyroid monitoring.
Soy, dietary fiber, walnuts and grapefruit can alter absorption; maintain a consistent routine and reassess after dietary changes.
Oral anticoagulants: thyroid correction can increase anticoagulant response; monitor coagulation and adjust treatment. Digoxin effects or levels can fall as euthyroidism is restored.
Insulin and glucose-lowering drugs: requirements can rise; monitor glucose.

Tricyclic/tetracyclic antidepressants, sympathomimetics and ketamine: cardiac or stimulatory toxicity can increase; monitor heart rate, pressure and symptoms. Sertraline may increase replacement requirements.

Rifampin, phenobarbital and tyrosine-kinase inhibitors can change requirements. Amiodarone and high-dose glucocorticoids or propranolol alter T4-to-T3 conversion. Estrogens, androgens, phenytoin and other binding modifiers can alter tests; interpret free hormone and clinical status.

Biotin can distort thyroid immunoassays. Stop biotin-containing supplements for at least 2 days before TSH or T4 testing, as directed by the label, and disclose their use to the laboratory and clinician.

Untreated maternal hypothyroidism poses maternal and fetal risks. Available clinical experience with replacement doses has not shown increased major birth defects or miscarriage. Continue treatment and promptly treat newly diagnosed disease; requirements commonly increase. Use trimester-specific TSH targets in primary disease and the pregnancy monitoring schedule above.

T4 is a normal milk constituent. Limited data on replacement therapy have not shown adverse infant effects. Adequate maternal treatment can improve low milk production caused by hypothyroidism. Continue individualized postpartum thyroid testing; some patients with Hashimoto disease need more than their pre-pregnancy dose.

Treat congenital disease promptly to protect growth and neurodevelopment. Follow both thyroid tests and growth/bone maturation; monitor infants for cardiac overload or arrhythmias during the first 2 weeks. Older adults need a reduced starting dose and careful cardiac assessment.

Levothyroxine has the physiological effects of endogenous T4. Peripheral deiodination supplies much of circulating T3; thyroid-hormone nuclear receptors regulate gene transcription and protein synthesis.
Oral absorption | Approximately 40–80%; fasting improves absorption, while food, medicines and malabsorption can reduce it.
Distribution / metabolism | More than 99% protein bound; deiodination plus glucuronide/sulfate conjugation.
Half-life / elimination | T4 half-life about 6–7 days when euthyroid, longer in hypothyroidism; renal and fecal elimination.
Primary hypothyroidism in adults: measure TSH 6–8 weeks after a dose change; once stable, reassess every 6–12 months and with clinical changes.
Central hypothyroidism: TSH is unreliable for dose adequacy. Follow free T4, aiming for the upper half of its normal range with clinical euthyroidism.

Children: check TSH and total/free T4 at 2 and 4 weeks after initiation, 2 weeks after a dose change, then every 3–12 months once stable until growth completes; assess development and bone maturation.
Assess pulse, cardiac symptoms, glucose and relevant anticoagulation; investigate adherence, timing and absorption before escalating an unexpectedly high dose.
Confirm the tablet strength in micrograms and follow one consistent dosing routine. Improvement takes weeks; replacement is often lifelong.
Tell the clinician about pregnancy, breastfeeding, supplements, heart disease and adrenal/pituitary disease. Stop biotin before tests as directed.
Report palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath, marked tremor or allergic symptoms promptly. Do not use thyroid hormone as a weight-loss medicine.
Dosage form / strength | Oral tablet · 50 mcg
Label packager | AbbVie Inc.
Appearance / imprint | White, round · SYNTHROID and 50
Example package NDC | 0074-4552-90 · Bottle of 90
Linked ready-to-use IV solution | 100, 200 or 500 mcg per 5 mL single-dose vial.
Other products | Oral liquid, capsule and injection products have separate labeling; do not apply tablet preparation instructions to them.
Store Synthroid at 20–25°C; excursions to 15–30°C are permitted. Protect from light and moisture. Follow the exact package instructions for other formulations.

assertions: The reviewed immediate-release tablets are labeled for adults and children aged 10 years and older with type 2 diabetes. The reviewed ER tablets are labeled for adults; their pediatric safety and effectiveness have not been established.

ADA 2026 supports considering prevention in adults at high diabetes risk, especially ages 25–59 with BMI ≥35 kg/m², higher fasting glucose or A1C, or previous gestational diabetes. It also discusses prevention of hyperglycemia in selected high-risk patients receiving PI3Kα inhibitors or high-dose glucocorticoids.

The international PCOS guideline supports selected metabolic uses, especially adult BMI ≥25 kg/m², and selected cycle-regulation uses with limited adolescent evidence. These are outside the reviewed U.S. diabetes indication and require an individualized plan.

Metformin does not treat diabetic ketoacidosis and is contraindicated in metabolic acidosis. The label does not establish conclusive macrovascular risk reduction; do not equate glucose lowering with proven cardiovascular protection for this product.
Starting dose | 500 mg twice daily or 850 mg once daily with meals.
Titration | Increase by 500 mg weekly or 850 mg every 2 weeks according to response/tolerability.
Maximum | 2,550 mg/day in divided doses; doses above 2,000 mg may be better tolerated in three doses with meals.
Swallow whole; do not cut, crush or chew. A missed ER dose should not be doubled or replaced with two doses that day; resume the usual next scheduled dose. Other ER brands have different labels.
Starting dose | 500 mg once daily with the evening meal.
Titration / usual maximum | Increase by 500 mg weekly, to 2,000 mg once daily with the evening meal.
If inadequate at 2,000 mg once daily | Label permits a trial of 1,000 mg twice daily. If a higher total is needed, switch to IR under clinician direction.
Switch from IR | Same daily total up to 2,000 mg once daily; verify the exact ER product.

Start 500 mg twice daily with meals. Increase by 500 mg weekly if needed and tolerated; maximum 2,000 mg/day in two divided doses. This schedule does not establish pediatric use of the reviewed ER product.
Check eGFR before treatment and periodically. The label provides no standard dose-reduction formula for continued therapy below 45. Avoid use in hepatic impairment because of lactic-acidosis risk.
Below 30 | Contraindicated; discontinue.
30–45 | Starting therapy is not recommended.
Falls below 45 during therapy | Reassess the benefit and risk of continuing.

Hold at or before iodinated contrast if eGFR is 30–60, there is a history of liver disease, alcoholism or heart failure, or contrast is intra-arterial. Recheck eGFR after 48 hours and restart only if stable. Temporarily stop while surgical/procedural food and fluid intake is restricted; agree the restart plan with the treating team.

For PCOS, the guideline suggests a low starting dose and 500 mg increases every 1–2 weeks, with suggested ceilings of 2.5 g/day in adults and 2 g/day in adolescents. This does not confer pediatric ER approval. Prevention regimens should follow the selected guideline and clinician plan rather than a universal diabetes-label maximum.

Accumulation and lactic acidosis risk rise with renal dysfunction, hypoxic illness, hepatic disease, excess alcohol, some interacting drugs and older age. Stop for shock, sepsis, acute myocardial infarction or hypoxic/hypoperfused acute heart failure.

The September 2026 label advises against use in mitochondrial diseases such as MELAS or maternally inherited diabetes and deafness; discontinue if elevated lactate develops and evaluate the clinical context.

New unexplained severe weakness, muscle pain, abdominal symptoms, rapid/deep breathing or unusual sleepiness may signal lactic acidosis. Stop metformin and seek immediate care; hospital treatment and prompt hemodialysis may be needed.
eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m².
Hypersensitivity to metformin.
Acute or chronic metabolic acidosis, including diabetic ketoacidosis with or without coma.

Metformin-associated lactic acidosis has been fatal. The boxed warning lists renal and hepatic dysfunction, contrast, surgery, hypoxic states, excessive alcohol, mitochondrial disease and selected interactions among important risk factors.

Diarrhea, nausea/vomiting and other gastrointestinal symptoms are common; IR and ER trial frequencies differ and are not interchangeable. Long-term therapy can lower vitamin B12. Insulin or secretagogue combinations can cause hypoglycemia. Postmarketing liver injury has been reported. Suspected overdose requires urgent assessment; contact U.S. Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.
Carbonic-anhydrase inhibitors such as topiramate, zonisamide and acetazolamide promote acidosis: consider more frequent monitoring.
Renal transporter inhibitors such as cimetidine, dolutegravir, ranolazine and vandetanib increase metformin exposure: assess the benefit and lactic-acidosis risk.
Alcohol impairs lactate handling: avoid excessive acute or chronic intake.
Insulin or sulfonylureas increase hypoglycemia risk: their doses may need reduction.
Corticosteroids, thiazides, thyroid hormones and other hyperglycemia-promoting medicines can worsen control: monitor glucose when starting and for hypoglycemia when withdrawing them.

Available human studies have not shown a clear major-malformation or miscarriage signal, but the label considers the data insufficient to exclude risk. Poor glucose control itself carries substantial risk. ADA 2026 prefers insulin for type 2 diabetes and gestational diabetes in pregnancy; metformin crosses the placenta and is not a first-line pregnancy agent. Review treatment with the obstetric team.

Milk exposure is low. LactMed reports infant intake generally below 0.5% of the maternal weight-adjusted dose and no adverse effects in one sizeable prospective study; timing feeds around doses adds little benefit. Use extra caution for newborn, premature or renally impaired infants. The label notes limited infant-outcome data; weigh maternal need and infant factors.
Metformin can restore ovulation in some previously anovulatory premenopausal patients, creating a possibility of unintended pregnancy. Discuss contraception and pregnancy intentions.

IR use below age 10 and pediatric use of this ER product are not established. Start cautiously in older adults and check renal function more often. Renal dysfunction increases accumulation; hepatic impairment is a reason to avoid use even though metformin is not hepatically metabolized.

Metformin lowers basal and post-meal glucose through reduced hepatic glucose production and intestinal glucose absorption and improved peripheral insulin sensitivity. It does not increase insulin secretion.
Absorption | IR 500 mg fasting bioavailability approximately 50–60%; ER median peak about 7 hours. Food effects differ by formulation.
Metabolism / distribution | No identified human metabolites; negligible plasma-protein binding and red-cell distribution.
Elimination | Unchanged renal excretion, including tubular secretion; plasma half-life about 6.2 hours and blood half-life about 17.6 hours. Renal impairment prolongs elimination.
Check glucose control and HbA1c according to the diabetes plan; assess tolerability during titration.
Obtain eGFR before treatment and at least annually; test more often in older adults or those at risk of renal decline and after relevant acute illness.
Measure hematologic parameters annually and vitamin B12 every 2–3 years under this label; investigate anemia or neuropathy sooner.
Review acute illness, dehydration, hypoxia, hepatic disease, alcohol and new interactions; monitor combination-associated hypoglycemia.
Take with the prescribed meal schedule. ER tablets must remain whole; their inactive shell may appear in stool.
Report persistent gastrointestinal intolerance. Do not double a missed ER dose.
Tell procedural teams about metformin before contrast or surgery. Follow a clinician-provided hold/restart plan for restricted intake or acute illness.
Know lactic-acidosis warning symptoms and seek urgent care. Learn hypoglycemia recognition and treatment when also using insulin or a secretagogue.

assertions: Treatment of hypertension, alone or with other antihypertensives. Coronary indications include chronic stable angina and vasospastic angina, alone or with other antianginal medicines.

In angiographically documented coronary artery disease without heart failure or ejection fraction below 40%, Norvasc is indicated to reduce hospitalization for angina and the risk of coronary revascularization. This indication does not establish a mortality benefit.

Regular therapy helps prevent angina but does not relieve an attack already in progress. Follow the prescribed rescue plan. This profile covers single-ingredient oral amlodipine; combination products require their own labels.

sections: Relevant section cited by this card

assertions: Hypertension
Start 5 mg once daily; maximum 10 mg once daily.
Small, frail, elderly, or hepatic impairment
May start 2.5 mg once daily for hypertension.
Chronic stable or vasospastic angina
5–10 mg once daily; use the lower dose initially in elderly patients or hepatic insufficiency.
Documented coronary artery disease
5–10 mg once daily.
Titration
Usually wait 7–14 days between changes; faster titration requires frequent assessment.

2.5–5 mg orally once daily. Doses above 5 mg daily have not been studied for this pediatric indication. Effects below age 6 are not established; the adult 10 mg maximum is not a pediatric recommendation.

Katerzia suspension and Norliqva solution each contain 1 mg/mL and have formulation-specific directions. Measure the prescribed dose with an oral syringe or dosing cup, never a household spoon. Shake Katerzia before every dose. Their storage requirements differ; see Product identification.

sections: How should this medicine be used?

assertions: Renal impairment does not significantly alter amlodipine pharmacokinetics; the usual initial dose can be used, subject to the patient’s other risks. Hepatic impairment reduces clearance: use a lower starting dose when appropriate and titrate slowly, especially in severe impairment.

Symptomatic hypotension is possible, particularly with severe aortic stenosis. Angina or myocardial infarction can occur after initiation or dose escalation, especially with severe obstructive coronary disease. Severe hepatic impairment requires slow titration.
Known sensitivity to amlodipine is a contraindication. Review the exact formulation’s ingredients when an excipient allergy is suspected.
The reviewed single-ingredient Norvasc label has no boxed warning. Its warnings about hypotension, coronary symptoms, and hepatic impairment still apply.

sections: Full prescribing information; no boxed warning

assertions: Peripheral edema is dose related. Dizziness, flushing, and palpitations can also occur; fatigue, nausea, abdominal pain, and somnolence were reported in trials. Rare postmarketing reports include jaundice or elevated liver enzymes; report jaundice promptly. Trial rates and voluntary reports do not establish an individual patient’s risk.

Overdose may produce severe, prolonged hypotension and requires immediate medical assessment. Call U.S. Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222; call 911 for collapse, seizure, difficulty breathing, or inability to awaken.

sections: How should this medicine be used?

assertions: Moderate or strong CYP3A inhibitors can increase exposure: monitor hypotension and edema; a lower amlodipine dose may be needed.
CYP3A inducers: monitor blood pressure closely because the quantitative interaction is uncertain.
Simvastatin: limit to 20 mg daily with amlodipine.
Cyclosporine or tacrolimus: check trough levels frequently and adjust the immunosuppressant as needed.
Sildenafil: monitor for additive hypotension.

Human pregnancy data are insufficient to define risks of birth defects or miscarriage. Poorly controlled maternal hypertension also carries risk. Review treatment with the obstetric clinician rather than changing therapy without a plan.

Amlodipine enters milk. The label reports limited infant observations without adverse effects and no information on milk production. Current LactMed considers milk levels usually low and says required maternal treatment is not a reason to stop breastfeeding. Evidence remains limited; individualize care for the infant.

Pediatric hypertension dosing is established for ages 6–17, with a studied limit of 5 mg daily. Elderly patients may clear amlodipine more slowly; start cautiously at the lower end and reassess blood pressure, symptoms, and edema.

Hepatic insufficiency increases exposure and may require 2.5 mg initially for hypertension with slow titration. Renal failure alone does not require the same adjustment. Other clinical factors can still justify a lower dose.

Amlodipine inhibits calcium entry, predominantly in vascular smooth muscle. Reduced peripheral resistance lowers blood pressure; reduced afterload and inhibition of coronary spasm contribute to antianginal effects. Chronic oral dosing generally does not substantially change heart rate.
Absorption
Peak plasma levels about 6–12 hours after an oral dose; food does not alter bioavailability.
Metabolism
Extensive hepatic conversion to inactive metabolites.
Elimination
Terminal half-life about 30–50 hours; steady state after 7–8 days. Renal impairment has little effect, whereas hepatic impairment prolongs elimination.
Assess blood pressure and symptoms after initiation and dose changes; monitor edema, dizziness, and palpitations.
Reassess new or worsening angina immediately.
When interacting medicines are started or stopped, reassess blood pressure; obtain transplant-drug trough levels when relevant.
Take once daily at a consistent time, with or without food, and continue as prescribed even when feeling well.

assertions: Stop promptly when pregnancy is detected. Angioedema can occur at any time, may obstruct the airway, and requires immediate discontinuation and urgent assessment. Intestinal angioedema can cause abdominal pain with or without nausea or vomiting.

Volume depletion, diuretics, heart failure, renal disease, or renal artery stenosis increase the risk of hypotension or acute kidney injury. Monitor renal function and potassium; reassess treatment for clinically significant deterioration. Rare cholestatic hepatitis can progress to liver failure: stop and evaluate jaundice or marked liver enzyme elevations.
Prior ACE inhibitor-related angioedema or hypersensitivity; hereditary or idiopathic angioedema.
Concurrent neprilysin inhibitor therapy. Do not give lisinopril within 36 hours before or after sacubitril/valsartan.
Aliskiren together with lisinopril in a patient with diabetes.
The label warns that medicines acting on the renin–angiotensin system can injure or kill a developing fetus. Discontinue as soon as pregnancy is detected.

Cough, dizziness, headache, and hypotension can occur; renal dysfunction and hyperkalemia require laboratory assessment. Rare neutropenia is reported: assess fever or sore throat. Tell the care team before surgery or anesthesia. Life-threatening anaphylactoid reactions have occurred with certain high-flux dialysis membranes, LDL apheresis, and venom desensitization.
Sacubitril/valsartan or other neprilysin inhibitors: contraindicated overlap; at least 36 hours separating lisinopril and sacubitril/valsartan in either direction.
ARBs or aliskiren: generally avoid dual RAS blockade. Aliskiren is contraindicated with diabetes and should be avoided with GFR <60 mL/min.
Potassium supplements, potassium salt substitutes, or potassium-sparing diuretics: increased hyperkalemia risk; monitor potassium frequently if a combination is needed.
Diuretics: volume depletion can cause excessive hypotension; clinician-directed dose adjustment may be required.
NSAIDs, including selective COX-2 inhibitors: reduced antihypertensive effect and possible renal injury; monitor renal function, particularly with dehydration or impaired kidneys.
Lithium: possible toxicity; monitor serum lithium.
Insulin or oral antidiabetics: increased hypoglycemia risk; monitor closely, particularly during the first month.
mTOR inhibitors: increased angioedema risk. Injectable gold: rare flushing, nausea, vomiting, and hypotension reactions.

Do not use during pregnancy. Exposure, particularly in the second and third trimesters, can cause fetal renal failure, oligohydramnios, pulmonary or skeletal complications, and death. Stop promptly and arrange replacement therapy when pregnancy is detected. In-utero exposure warrants specialist fetal and neonatal assessment.

The reviewed Zestril label states that human milk data are unavailable and advises women not to breastfeed during treatment. LactMed’s July 2026 review incorporates a five-woman study with very low milk transfer and considers adverse effects unlikely. Infant blood-level data remain unavailable; observations are small and do not establish safety for every infant. Discuss this discrepancy and treatment alternatives with the prescribing and infant-care clinicians.

Hypertension efficacy and safety were established in ages 6–16; the labeled indication and dosing apply to children 6 years and older with the renal limitations above. Pediatric heart failure or post-MI regimens are not established in this label. Age alone does not mandate a dose change in older adults, but renal function, volume status, and tolerability guide dosing.

Renal clearance drives exposure; reduce the starting dose at CrCl ≤30 mL/min or with hemodialysis. Renal artery stenosis or volume depletion increases acute kidney injury risk. No separate hepatic dosing schedule is supplied; promptly evaluate hepatic warning signs.

Inhibition of ACE reduces angiotensin II formation and aldosterone secretion, lowering vascular resistance. ACE also degrades bradykinin. Blood pressure lowering begins about 1 hour after dosing and peaks around 6 hours; individual responses vary.
Absorption
Mean oral absorption about 25%, with wide variability; food does not alter bioavailability.
Peak / effective half-life
Peak serum concentration around 7 hours; effective half-life with repeated dosing about 12 hours.
Metabolism / elimination
Not metabolized; excreted unchanged in urine. Renal impairment increases exposure, especially below GFR 30 mL/min; hemodialysis can remove lisinopril.
Assess blood pressure, creatinine or eGFR, potassium, and volume status before treatment and after changes.

For CKD, KDIGO advises checking blood pressure, creatinine, and potassium within 2–4 weeks of initiation or dose increase, adjusted to baseline GFR and potassium. Higher-risk or symptomatic patients need closer assessment.
In CKD, a creatinine rise >30% within 4 weeks warrants evaluation and treatment reassessment; assess dehydration, NSAIDs, and other reversible contributors.
Follow heart failure symptoms or post-MI hemodynamics as appropriate; monitor glucose more closely with antidiabetic therapy and lithium levels with lithium.
Report pregnancy immediately; discuss an alternative before a planned pregnancy.
Stop and seek emergency care for lip, tongue, throat, or facial swelling, especially with breathing or swallowing difficulty.
Discuss potassium supplements, salt substitutes, and OTC NSAIDs before use. Report fainting, vomiting, diarrhea, or dehydration.
Take at the same time daily. If a dose is missed, take it when remembered unless nearly time for the next; skip then and never double.
Use an oral syringe for liquid. Tell surgical, dialysis, and desensitization teams about lisinopril.

assertions: The selected OTC nasal products relieve nasal allergy symptoms. Propionate Flonase Allergy Relief is for age 4 and older; furoate Flonase Sensimist is for age 2 and older. Both include itchy, watery eye relief in their age 12-and-older directions. Nasal products are not asthma treatment.

The selected propionate HFA inhaler is labeled for asthma maintenance from age 4; furoate Arnuity Ellipta from age 5. Neither treats an acute attack. This reference covers these four single-ingredient products; other devices, prescription nasal indications, and combination inhalers need their own labels.

Doses below are sprays into EACH nostril once daily. Shake propionate gently and Sensimist vigorously before use; prime and clean according to the specific package instructions. Adults should supervise children. Use the least dose that controls symptoms.
Propionate 50 mcg/spray, age ≥12 | Week 1: 2 sprays; weeks 2–6 months: 1 or 2. Consult a clinician after 6 months of daily use.
Propionate, age 4–11 | 1 spray; shortest needed duration. Ask the child’s clinician if use exceeds 2 months/year. Do not use under age 4.
Furoate 27.5 mcg/spray, age ≥12 | Week 1: 2 sprays; weeks 2–6 months: 1 or 2. Consult a clinician after 6 months of daily use.
Furoate, age 2–11 | 1 spray; shortest needed duration. Ask the child’s clinician if use exceeds 2 months/year. Do not use under age 2.

For age ≥12 not previously using an inhaled corticosteroid, the starting dose is 88 mcg twice daily, approximately 12 hours apart; prior therapy and severity determine other starting regimens. The maximum labeled dose is 880 mcg twice daily. Age 4–11: 88 mcg twice daily (two 44-mcg actuations each time). Titrate to the lowest effective dose after stability; full benefit may take 2 weeks or longer.

Arnuity: age ≥12 not using an inhaled corticosteroid starts 100 mcg once daily; prior therapy/severity affect other starts. If response is inadequate after 2 weeks, consider 200 mcg once daily, the maximum for this age group. Age 5–11: 50 mcg once daily. Take one actuation at the same time each day, no more than once every 24 hours.

HFA: shake for 5 seconds before each spray. Prime with four sprays before first use; prime with one spray if unused for more than 7 days or dropped. A valved holding chamber, with a mask when appropriate, can help young children. Ellipta: opening the cover prepares one dose; exhale away from the device, inhale steadily and deeply through the mouthpiece, and do not block its air vent. After either asthma inhaler, rinse the mouth and spit out the water.

Asthma inhalers can cause thrush, infection susceptibility, adrenal suppression, reduced bone density, impaired growth, glaucoma/cataracts, and paradoxical bronchospasm. Worsening breathing immediately after a dose requires stopping that inhaler and urgent assessment with appropriate rescue treatment. Exposure to chickenpox or measles and existing infections need clinician review. During systemic-steroid reduction, the propionate HFA label also calls for assessment of eosinophilia, vasculitic rash, worsening lung symptoms, cardiac complications, or neuropathy; causality is unestablished. Transfer from systemic steroids requires supervised tapering; adrenal insufficiency may emerge during illness or surgery.

Nasal labels caution against use before nasal injury/surgery heals. Review recurrent severe nosebleeds, a whistling nasal sound, vision changes, or symptoms unimproved after 7 days. Children may grow more slowly. Seek assessment after exposure to chickenpox, measles, or tuberculosis. Use all corticosteroids together only after medication review.

Do not use a product after hypersensitivity to its ingredients. Both asthma inhalers are contraindicated as primary treatment of status asthmaticus or acute episodes needing intensive care. Arnuity contains lactose with milk proteins and is contraindicated in severe milk-protein allergy. Nasal OTC labels additionally say not to use below their respective age limits, for asthma, or with unhealed nasal injury/surgery.
These selected labels do not contain a boxed warning. Their adrenal, infection, growth, eye, and hypersensitivity warnings remain clinically important.

Nasal irritation, stinging, and bleeding can occur. Inhaled products commonly report upper respiratory symptoms, throat irritation, headache, or oral candidiasis; serious hypersensitivity is possible. Chronic excessive dosing or inhibited metabolism can cause systemic steroid effects and adrenal suppression. Do not add extra maintenance doses for an attack; suspected overdose or systemic steroid toxicity requires assessment.

assertions: Propionate HFA labeling advises against strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, including ritonavir and strong azole inhibitors, because systemic exposure and adrenal toxicity may increase. Arnuity advises caution with strong inhibitors, including ritonavir and ketoconazole. Nasal OTC labels require clinician/pharmacist review with HIV medicines such as ritonavir or oral ketoconazole. This is not an identical prohibition for every formulation.

Reconcile oral, injected, nasal, inhaled, and topical steroids. Nasal labels specifically direct review of other steroid medicines. Inhaler labels caution that systemic-steroid withdrawal and total corticosteroid exposure require individualized management.

Nasal labels advise consultation during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Both asthma labels have insufficient human pregnancy data and emphasize the risks of poorly controlled asthma. Human milk data are unavailable for these inhaled ingredients; HFA labeling notes that low plasma concentrations suggest low milk levels. Balance breastfeeding benefits, maternal treatment needs, and potential infant effects rather than declaring proven safety.

Respect the separate nasal and inhaler ages and doses above; monitor pediatric growth and use the lowest effective dose. Older adults need attention to bone and eye risks. Arnuity requires no age-based geriatric dose adjustment; individual inhaler selection also depends on the ability to use the device.

Arnuity requires no renal or mild hepatic dose adjustment; moderate/severe hepatic impairment increases systemic exposure, warranting caution and monitoring for steroid effects. Pediatric hepatic effects were not evaluated. Formal renal/hepatic PK studies were not performed for propionate HFA; its hepatic clearance supports closer monitoring with liver disease. The selected OTC nasal labels provide no organ-specific numeric regimen.

Both esters activate glucocorticoid pathways and reduce inflammatory activity. Their asthma benefit develops with regular use and may take 1–2 weeks or longer to maximize. Receptor-binding comparisons do not establish a clinical dose equivalence.

Swallowed propionate has very low oral bioavailability, but drug delivered to the lung can enter systemic circulation. Propionate and furoate undergo hepatic CYP3A4 metabolism. Furoate inhalation has an approximately 24-hour elimination phase half-life after repeated dosing; these kinetics do not justify swapping the nasal and pulmonary regimens.

Check control, reliever use, exacerbations, adherence, and device technique before stepping up treatment. GINA 2026 prefers an ICS–formoterol reliever strategy for many adults/adolescents; alternatives use a maintenance controller with a separate reliever. Fluticasone alone is not an ICS–formoterol rescue or maintenance-and-reliever inhaler. Coordinate the prescribed reliever and action plan with the clinician.

sections: Summary guide pp. 14, 21–25 / treatment tracks and reassessment

assertions: Demonstrate the exact nasal or inhaler technique; inspect dose counters and do not exceed labeled use. Check thrush, eye symptoms, growth, and systemic steroid effects as appropriate. Seek urgent care for severe breathing difficulty or allergy. A nasal spray that fails after a week or requires prolonged pediatric use needs review; persistent asthma symptoms need controller reassessment.

Examples are Flonase Allergy Relief propionate nasal spray, Flonase Sensimist furoate nasal spray, Prasco propionate HFA authorized generic, and Arnuity Ellipta furoate powder. The HFA product uses an orange actuator and peach cap (44-mcg, 120-actuation package NDC 66993-078-96); Arnuity uses a light-gray/orange inhaler (50-mcg, 30-blister package NDC 0173-0888-10). Appearance can vary across manufacturers; verify the package and dose counter.

Selected strengths: propionate nasal 50 mcg/spray; furoate nasal 27.5 mcg/spray; propionate HFA 44, 110, or 220 mcg per actuation (120 metered actuations); Arnuity 50, 100, or 200 mcg per blister. The 50-mcg Arnuity pack has 30 blisters; 100/200 also have 14-dose institutional packs. These are different formulations, not a substitution table.

Propionate nasal: 4–30°C. Sensimist: 15–30°C; do not refrigerate or freeze. HFA: 20–25°C, excursions 15–30°C, mouthpiece down; protect from excessive heat, do not puncture/incinerate, and discard at counter 000. Arnuity: 20–25°C, excursions 15–30°C, dry and protected from heat/sunlight; keep sealed in its tray until use and discard 6 weeks after opening or at counter 0, whichever comes first. Use each inhaler with its own supplied device components.

assertions: Flomax treats signs and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia. It is not labeled to treat hypertension. Evaluate the cause of urinary symptoms because BPH and prostate cancer can coexist.

EAU 2026 offers alpha blockers as an off-label option for selected patients with distal ureteral stones 5–10 mm. Use only when active removal is not indicated and the patient understands the tradeoffs. Stop conservative treatment if infection, refractory pain, or worsening renal function develops. This guideline does not establish a U.S. tamsulosin approval or a universal stone-treatment dose.

Take 0.4 mg once daily about 30 minutes after the same meal each day. If response is insufficient after 2–4 weeks, the prescriber may increase to 0.8 mg once daily. If either regimen is interrupted for several days, restart with 0.4 mg once daily. Swallow capsules whole; do not open, crush, or chew.

No renal dose adjustment is specified, but CrCl below 10 mL/min/1.73 m² was not studied. Moderate hepatic impairment requires no adjustment; severe impairment was not studied. Review hypotension risk and interacting medicines before increasing to 0.8 mg.

Postural dizziness, hypotension, and syncope can occur; protect against falls especially when starting or restarting. Current or previous exposure can cause intraoperative floppy iris syndrome during cataract/glaucoma surgery. Do not start when such surgery is scheduled; the benefit of stopping beforehand is unproven, so coordinate rather than choosing a washout. A painful persistent erection needs immediate treatment. Screen for prostate cancer before therapy and periodically. Use caution after serious or life-threatening sulfonamide allergy.

Known hypersensitivity to tamsulosin or any capsule component is a contraindication. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor combinations are directed against under dosage/warnings rather than listed in the formal contraindications section.
The selected U.S. label contains no boxed warning. Its syncope, interaction, priapism, and surgical warnings still require action.

Dizziness, abnormal ejaculation, rhinitis, and fatigue are reported in trials. Postmarketing reports include hypersensitivity, severe skin reactions, hypotension, arrhythmias, and IFIS; spontaneous reports cannot establish frequency. Excess dosing can cause marked hypotension requiring cardiovascular support, fluids or vasopressors as appropriate, and renal monitoring. Dialysis is unlikely to help because protein binding is high.

Do not combine with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole. Use caution with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin), strong/moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine/terbinafine), known CYP2D6 poor metabolism, and cimetidine—especially above 0.4 mg. Simultaneous inhibition of both pathways may substantially increase exposure.

Do not combine with another alpha blocker. PDE5 inhibitors can produce symptomatic hypotension; review the combination and monitor. Warfarin interaction studies are inconclusive, and the label recommends caution rather than a predictable dose change.

Flomax is not indicated for women. Human pregnancy-risk and milk/infant-effect data are inadequate or absent; animal findings do not establish human safety. Ejaculatory changes can affect sexual function, and label fertility effects are based on animal studies, not a quantified human infertility risk. Off-label treatment during pregnancy or lactation requires a separate assessment.

There is no pediatric indication; trials in children with neurologic bladder dysfunction did not demonstrate efficacy. Older adults showed no overall trial difference, but greater sensitivity remains possible, warranting attention to dizziness and falls.

Renal impairment generally needs no dose adjustment; end-stage renal disease below CrCl 10 mL/min/1.73 m² remains unstudied. Moderate hepatic impairment needs no adjustment; no severe-hepatic regimen is established by the label.

Tamsulosin preferentially blocks alpha-1 receptors in the prostate, reducing the dynamic smooth-muscle component of bladder outlet obstruction and improving urine flow and BPH symptoms. This mechanism does not make it an approved antihypertensive.

Food changes absorption, supporting consistent meal timing. The drug is highly protein bound and metabolized mainly through CYP3A4 and CYP2D6. Less than 10% is excreted unchanged in urine. The apparent half-life with Flomax capsules is about 9–13 hours in healthy volunteers and 14–15 hours in the target population.

Assess urinary symptoms, response after the initial 2–4 weeks, blood-pressure symptoms, and medication interactions. Perform prostate-cancer assessment before treatment and periodically. Ask about cataract/glaucoma surgery, falls, severe sulfa allergy, and prior alpha-blocker exposure.

Rise carefully and avoid hazardous activities until the effect is known. Report fainting, troublesome ejaculation changes, or worsening urinary symptoms. Seek immediate help for a persistent painful erection, severe allergy, or severe skin reaction. Inform the eye surgeon even if treatment ended long ago. After several missed days contact the prescriber to resume the 0.4-mg regimen.

The source label describes Flomax 0.4-mg hard gelatin capsules with an olive-green cap and orange body, marked “Flomax 0.4 mg” and “BI 58.” The source manufacturer package is a 100-capsule bottle, NDC 0024-5837-01. The retrieved DailyMed record is a RedPharm repackaged label with its own NDC; its packaging should not be conflated with that source bottle. Other generic appearances vary.

The selected U.S. Flomax product is a 0.4-mg capsule; a 0.8-mg regimen uses two capsules. Do not treat different formulations or non-U.S. product strengths as interchangeable without checking their specific label.
Store at 25°C (77°F); excursions of 15–30°C (59–86°F) are permitted. Keep out of children’s reach and preserve capsules intact until use.

assertions: Eliquis reduces stroke/systemic embolism risk in adult nonvalvular AF; prevents DVT after adult hip or knee replacement; treats adult DVT and PE; and reduces recurrent DVT/PE risk after initial treatment. These uses have separate dosing and treatment-duration requirements.

Treatment of VTE and reduction of recurrence are approved from birth after at least 5 days of initial anticoagulant therapy. Pediatric use below 2.6 kg is not recommended because it was not studied. The pediatric approval does not extend adult AF or orthopedic-prophylaxis regimens to children.

The label does not recommend apixaban for prosthetic heart valves or triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome. It is not an alternative to unfractionated heparin for initial PE treatment with hemodynamic instability or anticipated thrombolysis/embolectomy.
Take orally twice daily. Food does not materially affect bioavailability. Select the regimen by indication.

rows: 5 mg twice daily; 2.5 mg twice daily only when ≥2 apply: age ≥80 years, weight ≤60 kg, serum creatinine ≥1.5 mg/dL
2.5 mg twice daily, starting 12–24 hours after surgery; 35 days after hip or 12 days after knee replacement
10 mg twice daily for the first 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily
2.5 mg twice daily after at least 6 months of DVT / PE treatment

assertions: Begin the apixaban regimen after at least 5 days of initial anticoagulation. The day numbers in this table refer to apixaban treatment, not the preceding therapy. Reassess the weight tier as the child grows and individualize total duration. All entries below are twice-daily doses.

Adults and children ≥35 kg may use 2.5 or 5 mg tablets. They can be crushed into water, D5W or apple juice, or mixed with applesauce and promptly given. For a 12 French NG tube, suspend crushed tablets in 60 mL water or D5W and flush afterward with 20 mL. Stability of these crushed-tablet preparations is up to 4 hours; do not substitute this method for the pediatric packet/capsule instructions.

For 2.6 to <4 kg use the 0.15 mg Sprinkle capsules: open and mix the entire prescribed contents with water or infant formula; do not swallow the capsule. For 4 to <35 kg use 0.5 mg tablets supplied in packets; mix with water, formula, apple juice or applesauce, not swallowed whole. Liquid mixtures must be administered within 2 hours; applesauce mixtures immediately. Use the exact IFU volumes, oral syringe and rinse steps to deliver the full dose. The 0.5 mg packet-tablet liquid mixture has specified NG/G-tube options; obtain tube-size and preparation instructions rather than extrapolating to Sprinkle capsules.

Take a missed dose as soon as possible on the same day and resume twice-daily dosing; never double. For a child vomiting or spitting up within 30 minutes, repeat the dose; after more than 30 minutes, do not repeat and give the next scheduled dose. Repeated vomiting requires clinician advice.

The label calls for at least 48 hours of interruption before procedures with moderate/high bleeding risk, or at least 24 hours for low-risk procedures with readily controlled bleeding. Bridging during this short interruption is generally unnecessary; restart once adequate hemostasis is established. Neuraxial procedures require a separate anesthesia plan; these general surgical intervals are not a complete neuraxial protocol.

From warfarin, start apixaban when INR is below 2.0. Apixaban affects INR during the reverse transition; one labeled approach starts both warfarin and a parenteral anticoagulant when the next apixaban dose would be due, stopping the parenteral drug when INR is acceptable. For transitions with other oral/parenteral anticoagulants, start the replacement at the next scheduled dose time. Use a supervised plan to avoid gaps or unintended overlap.

Serious or fatal bleeding can occur; stop apixaban for active pathological hemorrhage and assess promptly. Other antithrombotics, NSAIDs and SSRIs/SNRIs can increase bleeding risk. Premature cessation without alternative anticoagulation increases thrombotic risk.

Neuraxial hematoma may cause permanent paralysis. The label specifies no catheter removal earlier than 24 hours after the last dose, no next dose earlier than 5 hours after removal, and a 48-hour delay after traumatic puncture. These are label precautions, not a complete anesthesia protocol; optimal timing is not established and pediatric catheter timing has no supporting data. New leg weakness/numbness or bowel/bladder dysfunction needs urgent evaluation.

Active pathological bleeding and severe hypersensitivity to apixaban or the product are contraindications. Renal/hepatic and indication-specific restrictions require additional review even when they are not formal contraindications.

sourceAudit.card: Boxed warning · Thrombosis and spinal hematoma
assertions: The boxed warning addresses increased thrombosis after premature discontinuation and spinal/epidural hematoma with neuraxial anesthesia or spinal puncture. Risk rises with indwelling catheters, other hemostasis-altering drugs, traumatic/repeated puncture and spinal deformity or surgery. Plan interruption and observe neurologic status.

Bleeding is the principal adult adverse reaction. Pediatric trial events commonly included headache, vomiting and excessive menstrual bleeding. Investigate blood loss, anemia or abnormal uterine bleeding rather than dismissing these as routine nuisance effects.

sourceAudit.card: Combined P-gp and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors
assertions: For adults taking 5 or 10 mg twice daily, reduce the apixaban dose by 50% with combined P-gp/strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole, itraconazole or ritonavir. Avoid these combinations when already taking 2.5 mg twice daily. Pediatric coadministration has not been studied; do not invent an adult-style weight-based adjustment. The label specifically states that clarithromycin does not require adjustment on pharmacokinetic grounds.

Avoid combined strong CYP3A4/P-gp inducers such as rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin and St. John’s wort: lower exposure can increase stroke or thrombosis risk. Antiplatelets, anticoagulants, thrombolytics, chronic NSAIDs and SSRIs/SNRIs increase bleeding risk and need an explicit benefit/risk review.

For AF, use the two-of-three reduction criteria rather than serum creatinine alone. For adult surgical prophylaxis and VTE, the label recommends no renal dose adjustment, including ESRD on dialysis; however, clinical studies excluded dialysis and CrCl below 15 mL/min, so those recommendations rely on PK/PD evidence. AF outcome equivalence on dialysis remains unknown.

Apixaban is not recommended at eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m² for age ≥2 years. For younger children, apply the label’s age-specific renal adequacy criteria; these are not the adult AF rule. The label table gives thresholds for both sexes: at 1 week, eGFR <8; at 2–8 weeks, <12; and after 8 weeks to <2 years, <22 mL/min/1.73 m². Specialist assessment is needed for neonatal ages not explicitly covered in that table.

Child-Pugh A needs no adjustment. No dosing recommendation can be provided for Child-Pugh B because of coagulation abnormalities and limited experience. Use is not recommended in Child-Pugh C; pediatric hepatic impairment has not been studied.

Use in pregnancy is not recommended; human data are limited and maternal/fetal bleeding is a concern. Discuss pregnancy plans and abnormal uterine bleeding. As delivery approaches, a shorter-acting anticoagulant may be considered under a coordinated obstetric/anticoagulation plan.

assertions: Breastfeeding is not recommended on apixaban. Although the product label retains an older absence-of-human-data statement, current LactMed documents substantial milk transfer and prefers an alternative, especially for newborn/preterm infants. Older adults still need the indication-specific dose criteria and assessment of organ function and interacting therapy.

Apixaban inhibits free and clot-bound factor Xa and prothrombinase activity without requiring antithrombin. PT/INR/aPTT changes at therapeutic doses are small and variable, making these tests unsuitable for routine assessment of anticoagulant effect. Specialized assays require a clinical question and local interpretation.

Oral bioavailability is about 50%, with peaks at 3–4 hours. Protein binding is about 87% and adult half-life about 12 hours. CYP3A4 is the main metabolic pathway; renal excretion contributes about 27% of total clearance, with intestinal/biliary elimination also contributing. The pediatric label reports a peak around 2 hours after a single dose; adult PK values must not replace pediatric weight-tier dosing.

Review the indication, dose, weight when relevant, renal/hepatic status, bleeding history and full medicine list. Follow bleeding or anemia symptoms and new interacting drugs. Do not stop without a plan; report blood in urine/stool, prolonged bleeding, faintness or neurologic symptoms. Tell dentists and procedural teams about treatment. Caregivers need hands-on preparation training and weight-tier review.

sourceAudit.card: Major bleeding and current reversal context
assertions: Anticoagulant effects can persist for at least 24 hours after a dose. Vitamin K and protamine do not reverse apixaban; dialysis has little effect. The current label allows consideration of PCC-based management but does not establish its clinical efficacy. FDA found Andexxa’s risks outweighed benefits and reported the end of U.S. sales on December 22, 2025; do not rely on older labels describing routine availability. Emergency specialists should use the current local protocol.

Suspected overdose or accidental ingestion requires urgent poison-center/medical assessment. Activated charcoal can reduce absorption in selected circumstances; this is a supervised toxicology decision, not a home treatment. Continue bleeding surveillance and supportive management.

Eliquis 5 mg tablets are pink, oval and biconvex with 894 / 5 imprints. Example bottle of 60: NDC 0003-0894-21. Pediatric packets and Sprinkle capsules have different strengths and preparation requirements; appearance alone does not establish the correct dose.

Adult/≥35 kg tablets contain 2.5 or 5 mg. Pediatric 0.5 mg tablets for suspension are supplied as packets containing 1, 3 or 4 tablets, corresponding to 0.5, 1.5 or 2 mg per packet. Sprinkle capsules contain 0.15 mg powder and are opened for suspension. Verify both tablet count and packet total.

Store Eliquis and Sprinkle at 20–25°C with excursions to 15–30°C. Follow formulation-specific mixture timing: pediatric liquids within 2 hours, applesauce mixtures immediately, and crushed 2.5/5 mg preparations up to 4 hours. Keep medicines away from children and use prescribed oral dosing equipment.

assertions: Simvastatin reduces mortality and coronary/cerebrovascular events and revascularization risk in defined high-risk adults with coronary, cerebrovascular or peripheral vascular disease and/or diabetes. It is used with diet for primary hyperlipidemia, HeFH, primary dysbetalipoproteinemia and hypertriglyceridemia; adult HoFH use is adjunctive to other LDL-lowering therapies.

The pediatric approval is for LDL reduction with diet in HeFH from age 10 years. Other pediatric lipid disorders and younger ages are not established uses. Current AHA/ACC guidance combines risk assessment, LDL/non-HDL goals and percentage reduction; if high-intensity therapy is required or goals remain unmet at 40 mg, the label directs an alternative LDL-lowering treatment.

Take orally once daily in the evening. Adults: the recommended range is 20–40 mg daily. HeFH from age 10: 10–40 mg daily. Reassess LDL-C as early as 4 weeks after initiation and adjust according to response, tolerance and interaction limits. A missed dose may be taken as soon as possible; do not double the next dose.

The usual recommended maximum is 40 mg daily. An 80 mg regimen is reserved for patients already taking 80 mg chronically, such as for at least 12 months, without muscle toxicity; do not start or titrate a patient to 80 mg. If an interacting drug is needed in someone on 80 mg, select another statin. Zocor no longer markets its 80 mg strength.

For severe renal impairment with creatinine clearance 15–29 mL/min, start at 5 mg once daily. Zocor’s 5 mg strength is no longer marketed, so select an appropriate alternative simvastatin tablet product. Mild/moderate renal impairment has no recommended dose adjustment, but all renal impairment increases muscle-toxicity risk. The cited dosing section does not establish a routine regimen for CrCl below 15.

Apply the exact co-medication cap even when the usual adult dose would be higher. Lomitapide’s legacy 40 mg exception is restricted to patients previously tolerating chronic 80 mg; it is not a new-start regimen.

rows: Reduce by 50%; maximum 20 mg daily, or restricted legacy 40 mg exception
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor; cyclosporine; danazol; gemfibrozil

assertions: The reviewed regimens refer to oral tablets. Marketed Zocor strengths are 10, 20 and 40 mg; generic labels also describe 5 and 80 mg tablets. Strength availability does not override dose restrictions. Liquid or combination products require their own label and administration/storage instructions.

Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis can cause kidney injury or death. Risk increases with higher doses, age ≥65, uncontrolled hypothyroidism, renal impairment and interacting medicines. Stop for suspected myopathy or markedly elevated CK. Serious illness with high rhabdomyolysis-related renal risk, such as sepsis, shock or major trauma, may require temporary cessation.

Persistent proximal weakness and elevated CK despite stopping can indicate immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy; stop and obtain specialist assessment. Consider baseline liver enzymes and repeat when clinically indicated; promptly stop for serious symptomatic liver injury, jaundice or hyperbilirubinemia. HbA1c/glucose can rise; maintain lifestyle and metabolic follow-up.

Strong CYP3A4 inhibitor coadministration, cyclosporine, danazol or gemfibrozil, acute liver failure/decompensated cirrhosis, and hypersensitivity to simvastatin or ingredients are contraindications. Pregnancy is no longer an absolute U.S. statin contraindication; the separate pregnancy risk assessment remains essential.
The reviewed simvastatin tablet labels do not carry an FDA boxed warning. This does not diminish the important muscle, interaction and hepatic precautions, including the restriction on 80 mg dosing.

Common reported trial events include headache, abdominal discomfort, constipation and nausea; upper respiratory infection was also commonly recorded. Serious postmarketing events include hepatic failure, immune-mediated myopathy and severe hypersensitivity. New or worsening myasthenia gravis and generally reversible cognitive symptoms have also been reported; spontaneous reports do not establish frequency or causation.

Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors include selected azoles (itraconazole, ketoconazole, posaconazole, voriconazole), macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin), boosted protease-inhibitor/cobicistat products and nefazodone. Suspend simvastatin for an unavoidable short course of a strong inhibitor. Cyclosporine, danazol and gemfibrozil are also contraindicated. Confirm the exact antiviral regimen rather than assuming every antiviral has the same interaction.

Observe the cardiac-drug and lomitapide caps above. Review temporary suspension during daptomycin treatment. Other fibrates, colchicine and lipid-modifying niacin doses (≥1 g/day) need benefit/risk review and muscle surveillance. Simvastatin with lipid-modifying niacin is not recommended in Chinese patients. Avoid grapefruit juice.

Obtain INR before initiating simvastatin with a coumarin anticoagulant, then check sufficiently often after starting, dose changes or discontinuation until stable. Simvastatin can increase digoxin concentrations; monitor levels when simvastatin is initiated.

assertions: Discontinue when pregnancy is recognized in most patients. FDA removed the blanket statin pregnancy contraindication in 2021 to permit individualized decisions for very high-risk patients, including HoFH or established cardiovascular disease. Available observational data do not show a clear increase in major malformations after adjustment, but miscarriage risk is uncertain and fetal harm remains possible. Discuss any exceptional continuation with specialists.

Breastfeeding is not recommended while taking simvastatin because of potential effects on infant cholesterol metabolism and limited infant safety evidence. Discuss temporarily withholding lipid treatment or an alternative feeding plan when continued therapy is necessary.

HeFH approval starts at age 10; trial girls were at least one year post-menarche. Do not impose an unverified approval for other pediatric lipid disorders or doses above 40 mg. Older adults have greater myopathy risk; choose doses cautiously and assess concomitant disease, renal function and medicines.

Monitor renal impairment for muscle toxicity and use the severe-renal starting-dose rule. Acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis is contraindicated; substantial alcohol use or liver history warrants assessment. The label reports greater myopathy risk in Chinese patients, particularly with niacin combinations; monitor and avoid the stated combination.
